title: Axiom released a machine-checked copy of the Stacks Project, about 16 million lines
friendlyTitle: Axiom published a computer-checked copy of a 7,500-page maths reference
summary: Axiom says it has released a Lean formalization of the entire Stacks Project, the open reference Johan de Jong started at Columbia in 2005. Axiom describes it as roughly 7,500 pages and some 16 million lines of code, and calls it the largest integrated, reusable library of formalized mathematics it knows of. The point is reuse: a later proof can import definitions and theorems instead of rebuilding schemes and cohomology. The browser at stacks.axiommath.ai shows the original text beside the Lean code. Axiom says the work surfaced dozens of statements that needed a local fix, including missing hypotheses and claims that did not hold as stated, and that agents built counterexamples for the breaks. This is a different release from the Classification of Finite Simple Groups formalization Axiom published on 27 October. de Jong has asked that AI-generated comments and pull requests not be sent to the upstream Stacks repository for now. Axiom says its formalization stays in its own repository.
friendlySummary: Axiom says it has released a Lean formalization of the whole Stacks Project. That project is an open maths reference Johan de Jong started at Columbia in 2005. Lean is a language where a program checks each step of a proof. Axiom describes the result as roughly 7,500 pages and about 16 million lines of code. It calls this the largest connected, reusable library of checked maths it knows of. The point is reuse. A later proof can import definitions and theorems instead of rebuilding the foundations. The site stacks.axiommath.ai shows the original text next to the Lean code. Axiom says the work found dozens of statements that needed a small fix, including missing assumptions and claims that were not true as written, and that its agents built counterexamples for the breaks. This is not the finite-groups proof Axiom published on 27 October. That was one big theorem. This is a library. de Jong has asked that AI-written comments and pull requests not be sent to the original Stacks repository for now. Axiom says its copy stays in its own repository.
whyItMatters: A checked library is useful only if the next proof can import it. If you work in Lean, the practical test is one theorem you already know, traced back to its Stacks tag, not the line count. If you do not work in Lean, this does not check a chatbot's maths answer. de Jong's request is the boundary: do not file the agent's comments on the original project.
